paragraphs.heading: Ripples in spacetime
paragraphs.text: Gravitational waves are ripples in the curvature of spacetime. They are made when masses move relative to one another, and they spread outward at the speed of light. Einstein predicted them from his general theory of relativity. They carry energy away as gravitational radiation, a kind of radiant energy similar to electromagnetic radiation.

paragraphs.heading: How they form
paragraphs.text: In general relativity, mass curves spacetime. When masses move, that curvature changes, and if the motion is not spherically symmetric, the changes travel outward as waves. Newton's gravity has no room for them, since it says gravity acts instantly everywhere. A passing wave changes the distances between freely falling masses, in a pattern that follows the shape of the wave. The size of this effect is inversely proportional to the distance from the source, not to the distance squared.

paragraphs.heading: Very small signals
paragraphs.text: Pairs of neutron stars spiralling into each other should be powerful sources, because their masses accelerate hugely as they orbit close together. Even so, they are so far away that the strain they cause on Earth is expected to be less than 1 part in 10²⁰. Catching it takes highly sensitive detectors at several sites. As of 2012, LIGO and Virgo were the most sensitive, working at about one part in 5×10²².

paragraphs.heading: First detections
paragraphs.text: The first evidence was indirect. In 1974 the orbit of the Hulse–Taylor binary pulsar was seen to decay at the rate general relativity predicts for energy lost to gravitational radiation, and Hulse and Taylor received the 1993 Nobel Prize in Physics for it. The first direct detection came in September 2015, when LIGO's detectors in Livingston, Louisiana, and Hanford, Washington, received a signal from two merging black holes. Rainer Weiss, Kip Thorne and Barry Barish shared the 2017 Nobel Prize for that work, and hundreds of these waves have been observed in all.

paragraphs.heading: A new way to look
paragraphs.text: Gravitational waves are not affected by matter lying in their path, since they do not interact strongly with it the way light does. That lets astronomers study exotic objects in the distant universe that optical and radio telescopes cannot see. The waves may even offer a view of the very early universe, which before recombination was opaque to electromagnetic radiation. Precise measurements also put general relativity to a more thorough test.

paragraphs.heading: As fast as light
paragraphs.text: In general relativity the waves travel at c, the speed of light in vacuum. In August 2017 LIGO and Virgo picked up a signal, GW170817, almost at the moment gamma-ray satellites and optical telescopes saw its source in the galaxy NGC 4993, about 130 million light years away. That limited any difference between the speed of gravitational waves and the speed of light to less than one part in 10¹⁵.

paragraphs.heading: Listening with pulsars
paragraphs.text: Waves of very low frequency can be found with pulsar timing arrays. Astronomers monitor the timing of about 100 pulsars spread across the Milky Way for years, watching for detectable changes in when their signals arrive. Waves from merging supermassive black holes, with wavelengths measured in light-years, can cause such changes, and this method has revealed the 'hum' of many such mergers. New detectors keep coming: Japan's KAGRA was completed in 2019, and the European Space Agency is developing a space-based observatory called LISA.
